content: 1. In 1987, point prevalence rates of scurvy were reported to be as high as 45% among females and 36% among males, with prevalence increasing with age. 2. The prevalence of scurvy was associated with the duration of residence in refugee camps and the length of time individuals were exposed to rations deficient in vitamin C. 3. A 1989 population survey of children under 5 years of age in Hartisheik camp in eastern Ethiopia found a clinical scurvy prevalence of 2%. 4. The international community has not developed an adequate strategy to prevent scurvy in refugee camps in the Horn of Africa, as evidenced by an outbreak among adult males (former Ethiopian soldiers) in a camp in eastern Sudan in 1991. 5. Pellagra is a condition caused by a severe deficiency of biologically available niacin in the diet. 6. Pellagra, once common in the southeastern United States, Italy, and Spain, now primarily occurs in maizeor sorghum-consuming populations in southern Africa, North Africa, and India. 7. An outbreak of pellagra occurred in Malawi among Mozambican refugees between July and October 1989. 8. Eleven camps reported a total of 1,169 pellagra patients, 20% of whom were children under 5 years of age. 9. The French agency Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) implemented active surveillance during this outbreak. 10. Another outbreak occurred between February and October 1990, with 17,878 cases reported among 285,942 refugees in the same 11 sites, resulting in an attack rate of 6.3%. 11. More than 18,000 cases of pellagra were reported across all districts hosting approximately 900,000 refugees in southern Malawi, with an overall attack rate of 2.0%. 12. Food rations during this outbreak contained an average of 4.9 mg of available niacin per person per day, whereas FAO/WHO recommendations for daily niacin intake range from 5.4 mg for infants to 20.3 mg for adults. 13. The outbreak occurred due to the failure of relief efforts to include an adequate supply of groundnuts (peanuts), the primary source of niacin in refugee rations. 14. The lack of variety in basic relief rations is a significant risk factor for pellagra and other micronutrient deficiency syndromes. 15. Treating maize flour with lime (which converts niacin to a biologically available form) and including beans, groundnuts, or fortified cereals in daily rations can increase the total intake of available niacin and prevent pellagra. 16. Anemia is highly prevalent in refugee and displaced populations, though it has been underreported in published literature. Unpublished CDC data suggest it is a serious problem in some areas. 17. A 1990 survey of Palestinian refugees in Syria, Jordan, and the West Bank revealed anemia prevalence rates of 50%-70% among infants and young children. 18. Anemia prevalence among nonpregnant and pregnant women was 25%-50%, while the male population showed a lower prevalence rate. 19. In this study, anemia was defined as a hemoglobin concentration of less than 11 g/dL in children and less than 12 g/dL in nonpregnant women. Pregnant women were considered anemic if their hemoglobin concentration was less than 11.5 g/dL during the first or third trimester, or less than 11.0 g/dL during the second trimester. 20. These findings suggest that iron deficiency, which disproportionately affects women and children, was the primary cause of anemia in this population. 21. A 1987 study among refugees in Somalia demonstrated anemia prevalence rates of 44%-71% among pregnant women, with higher rates observed in women in the third trimester of pregnancy. 22. The cutoff point for hemoglobin concentration in this study was 10 g/dL; using the WHO cutoff of 11 g/dL, the prevalence would have been even higher. 23. Among children aged 9-36 months, 59%-90% had hemoglobin levels below the 10 g/dL cutoff. 24. The inadequacy of general food rations was identified as the primary factor causing iron deficiency anemia in this population. 25. In a 1990 study, the anemia prevalence rate was 13% among children under 5 years of age in an Ethiopian camp for Somali refugees. 26. In addition to dietary iron deficiency, the high incidence of malaria in many refugee populations likely contributes to the high prevalence of anemia in children. 27. The high prevalence of anemia in some refugee populations may not be significantly greater than that found in local, non-refugee populations, as the latter group has been poorly documented. 28. Nevertheless, anemia may represent an additional preventable risk factor for high mortality in refugee populations. 29. Severe anemia (hemoglobin less than 5 g/dL) is often correlated with the high prevalence of anemia and can be a major cause of mortality among young children and pregnant women during the peripartum period. 30. Beriberi (thiamine deficiency) has been reported in several refugee populations subsisting on rice-based food rations, such as in Thailand (1980) and Guinea (1990). 31. Data on iodine deficiency in displaced populations are scarce, but anecdotal evidence suggests that iodine deficiency, as indicated by the presence of goiter, has been a problem in some camps in Pakistan and Ethiopia. 32. Measles, diarrheal diseases, acute respiratory infections (ARIs), and, in some cases, malaria are the primary causes of morbidity and mortality among refugee and displaced populations. 33. Densely populated camps with poor sanitation, inadequate clean water supplies, and low-quality housing contribute to the rapid spread of disease in refugee settings. 34. The interaction between malnutrition and infection, particularly among young children, has exacerbated the high rates of morbidity and mortality from communicable diseases in these populations. 35. Available and affordable technologies, such as immunization, adequate planning, sanitation, and appropriate case management (e.g., oral rehydration salts for diarrhea), could prevent much of this morbidity and mortality. 36. Measles outbreaks in refugee camps have been common and have caused significant mortality. 37. Low immunization coverage, combined with high rates of undernutrition and vitamin A deficiency, has played a critical role in the spread of measles and subsequent mortality in some refugee camps. 38. Measles has been one of the leading causes of death among children in refugee camps. 39. Measles infection can lead to or exacerbate vitamin A deficiency, compromising immunity and increasing susceptibility to xerophthalmia, blindness, and premature death. 40. In early 1985, the crude, measles-specific death rate in one eastern Sudan camp reached 13 per 1,000 per month; among children under 5 years of age, the measles-specific death rate was 30 per 1,000 per month. 41. Over 2,000 measles deaths were reported in this camp from February through the outbreak period.
